A smorgasbord is a large, varied mixture of things — a collection where there are many different types, all present together at once.

The single most important idea packed into this word is variety. Not just a few different things, but a generous, wide-ranging spread of many different kinds of things, all in one place.

This word has two meanings that build on each other.

1. The Literal Meaning (Food)

In its most direct sense, a smorgasbord is a style of meal — a big buffet table loaded with a large assortment of different dishes. Think of a long table at a party or restaurant covered with dozens of different foods: salads, meats, breads, hot dishes, cold dishes, soups, desserts — all laid out at once for people to walk up and help themselves, picking whatever they want.

The key features of this kind of meal are:

  • Many dishes, not just one or two
  • Many different types of food, not all the same category
  • Everything is available at once, all spread out together
  • You choose freely — you pick what appeals to you and ignore the rest

2. The Figurative Meaning (Everything Else — the Common Use)

This is the meaning you will encounter far more often in everyday English. Here, a smorgasbord is used to describe any large, diverse collection of things — not food at all.

Whenever someone wants to describe a rich, wide variety of things gathered together, they call it a smorgasbord. The word paints a picture of abundance and diversity in one shot.
The Exact Qualities That Make Something a "Smorgasbord"

For a collection of things to deserve the word smorgasbord, it typically needs to have all of these qualities:

Large in number — There has to be a lot. A smorgasbord is not two or three things. It implies a generous, almost overwhelming amount.

Diverse in type — The things must be genuinely different from each other, not just slight variations of the same thing. A collection of ten red pens is not a smorgasbord. A collection of pens, pencils, markers, crayons, chalk, and brushes is getting there.

All present together — The variety exists in the same place, at the same time. This is what gives the word its visual richness — you can imagine it all laid out before you.

Available for the picking — There is often a subtle sense that the person encountering a smorgasbord can choose what they want from it. The options are open to them.
Real Examples of How It's Used

Here are examples that show the word working in real sentences across different contexts:

Entertainment:
"The streaming platform offers a smorgasbord of content — thrillers, comedies, documentaries, anime, and reality shows."
(There is a huge variety of different types of shows to choose from.)

Ideas and opinions:
"The conference brought together a smorgasbord of viewpoints on climate change."
(Many different perspectives, all in one place.)

Emotions:
"Moving to a new country is a smorgasbord of feelings — excitement, fear, hope, and loneliness all at once."
(A rich mix of different emotions experienced together.)

Problems:
"The old computer had a smorgasbord of issues — a cracked screen, failing battery, broken keyboard, and corrupted files."
(Many varied problems at once.)

Learning:
"Her childhood home was a smorgasbord of languages — her parents spoke Spanish, her grandparents spoke Italian, and English was spoken at school."
The Tone and Feeling of the Word

Smorgasbord is not a neutral, clinical word. It carries a feeling of richness and abundance. When someone uses it, they are usually expressing a sense of being in front of something impressively vast and varied — almost like standing in front of a feast.

Because of this, the word tends to lean slightly positive or at least enthusiastic — it suggests there is plenty, perhaps even more than you expected. However, it can also be used in a mildly overwhelmed or even negative sense, when the sheer variety of something is too much to handle.

For example:

  • "The bookshop was a smorgasbord of wonderful reads." (positive, delighted)
  • "Navigating the healthcare system is a smorgasbord of confusing forms and rules." (negative, overwhelmed)
Register — When and Where This Word Is Used

Smorgasbord is a slightly elevated, expressive word. It is not slang, and it is not overly formal either. It sits comfortably in:

  • Everyday conversation between educated speakers
  • Journalism and magazine writing
  • Books and essays
  • Speeches and presentations

It is chosen when the speaker wants to be vivid and descriptive rather than plain. Instead of saying "a wide variety of things," using smorgasbord makes the sentence more colorful, more evocative, and more memorable. It is a word that does extra work — it doesn't just tell you there are many different things; it makes you picture them, all laid out before you at once.

To sharpen your understanding, here is what smorgasbord does not mean:

  • It does not mean a large quantity of the same thing. A thousand identical sandwiches is not a smorgasbord. Diversity is essential.
  • It does not mean things that are spread out over time. A smorgasbord exists all at once, in the same moment or place.
  • It does not specifically refer to chaos or disorder, though an overwhelming smorgasbord can feel that way. The word itself simply means variety and abundance — the emotional reaction to it depends on context.

If you had to reduce smorgasbord to its absolute essence:

A smorgasbord is a rich, generous, and diverse collection of many different things, all present together at once.

Every time you see or hear this word, that image — a table overflowing with countless different dishes, each one different from the last — is the feeling behind it, whether the subject is food, ideas, emotions, problems, or anything else.
